avl-tree-master/README.md:
# AVL Tree

**AVL Tree** is a Rust library implementing the self-balancing binary search tree with O(log n) guaranteed height, using height-balanced rotations (LL, RR, LR, RL) to maintain the AVL invariant after every insertion.

## Why It Matters

Plain binary search trees degrade to O(n) operations when fed sorted or near-sorted input — a common real-world scenario. AVL trees, invented by Adelson-Velsky and Landis in 1962, solve this by maintaining a strict balance invariant: the heights of the two child subtrees of any node differ by at most 1. This guarantees O(log n) worst-case height, making insert, search, and delete all O(log n). AVL trees are the data structure of choice when reads dominate writes, as their stricter balance (compared to red-black trees) yields shorter search paths. They are used in databases (SQLite B-tree internals use similar rebalancing), in-memory indexes, and any application requiring deterministic worst-case performance.

## How It Works

**The AVL Invariant:** For every node N:

```
|height(N.left) − height(N.right)| ≤ 1
```

After insertion, violations are detected via the **balance factor**:

```
BF(N) = height(N.right) − height(N.left)
```

Four violation cases and their fixes:

**Case 1: Left-Left (BF < −1, left child BF ≤ 0)**
```
     Z                Y
    / \              / \
   Y   T4   →      X     Z
  / \              / \   / \
 X   T3           T1 T2 T3 T4
/ \
T1 T2
```
Single right rotation on Z. O(1).

**Case 2: Right-Right (BF > 1, right child BF ≥ 0)**
Single left rotation on Z. Mirror of Case 1.

**Case 3: Left-Right (BF < −1, left child BF > 0)**
Left rotation on Y, then right rotation on Z. Two O(1) operations.

**Case 4: Right-Left (BF > 1, right child BF < 0)**
Right rotation on Y, then left rotation on Z. Mirror of Case 3.

**Height maintenance:** Each node stores its height. After insertion, heights are recomputed bottom-up during the recursive return. The height update is O(1) per node: `h = 1 + max(h_left, h_right)`.

**Complexity guarantees:**

| Operation | Time | Space |
|-----------|------|-------|
| insert | O(log n) | O(log n) stack |
| contains | O(log n) | O(1) |
| in_order traversal | O(n) | O(n) output |
| Height of tree | O(log n) guaranteed | — |

Maximum height for n nodes: h ≤ 1.44 × log₂(n + 2) − 0.328 (tight bound).

## Quick Start

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut tree = AvlTree::new();
    for &v in &[10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 25] {
        tree.insert(v);
    }
    assert!(tree.contains(&30));
    assert!(!tree.contains(&99));

    let sorted: Vec<&i32> = tree.in_order();
    println!("In-order: {:?}", sorted); // [10, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50]
}
```

## Architecture Notes

The AVL Tree provides **ordered index storage** within the SuperInstance fleet's conservation-law tracking system. When monitoring avoidance ratios across thousands of agents, the AVL tree enables O(log n) insertion of new observations and O(log n) lookup of historical values, supporting the real-time verification of γ + η = C conservation across the fleet.

See [ARCHITECTURE.md](https://github.com/SuperInstance/SuperInstance/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md).

**AVL vs Red-Black trees:** Red-Black trees (used in Java's TreeMap, C++'s std::map) maintain a weaker balance invariant: a node's black-height is the same on all root-to-leaf paths, but the overall height can be up to 2× log₂(n). AVL trees are more strictly balanced, resulting in shorter paths (faster lookups) but more rotations per insert/delete (slower modifications). Choose AVL when read-heavy, Red-Black when write-heavy. This implementation is AVL — optimized for the fleet's read-dominated access pattern (conservation-law lookups vastly outnumber insertions).

**Memory layout:** Each node stores: value (generic T), left/right child pointers (Option<Box>), height (usize). For T = u64, a node is 32 bytes on 64-bit systems. A tree of n = 1M entries uses ~32 MB. The boxed-pointer design avoids contiguous memory requirements, trading cache efficiency for allocation flexibility.
